title: Module 2.5 - Storing and accessing sequencing data II - Via command-line
text:
A second pass at the same material, for extra practice. The questions below are independent of Sections 1–4 above — you can run them in any empty working directory on HPC2N (or on your laptop where noted).



QE1.1 Create a directory called project/ with three sub-directories raw/, processed/ and results/ in a single command. Then create an empty file raw/sample.fastq and verify the structure with ls -R project.







Hint





mkdir -p creates parent directories as needed and does not complain if a directory already exists. You can list several paths on one mkdir line. touch creates an empty file.









Solution





mkdir -p project/raw project/processed project/results
touch project/raw/sample.fastq
ls -R project




QE1.2 You have the project/ tree from QE1.1. Make a backup copy of the whole project/ directory as project_backup/, then rename project_backup/raw/sample.fastq to sample_R1.fastq. Finally remove the backup completely.







Hint





cp -r src dst copies a directory recursively. mv both renames and moves. rm -r removes a directory and its contents — use rm -ri if you want to be prompted before each deletion.









Solution





cp -r project project_backup
mv project_backup/raw/sample.fastq project_backup/raw/sample_R1.fastq
rm -r project_backup







QE2.1 Run ls -l in a directory that contains a few files. Pick one file and read off the permission triplet (e.g. -rw-r--r--). Who can read it? Who can write it? Who can execute it?







Hint





The 10 characters break down as: type (1) + owner rwx (3) + group rwx (3) + others rwx (3). A - means the permission is not granted.









Solution





ls -l
# -rw-r--r--  means: regular file, owner can read+write, group can read, others can read.
# Nobody can execute it.




QE2.2 Create a small shell script hello.sh containing echo "hello", then make it executable only for the owner (not for the group or others), and run it as ./hello.sh.







Hint





chmod u+x file adds the execute bit for the user (owner). chmod 744 file would achieve a similar but stricter result: rwxr--r--. Check with ls -l hello.sh.









Solution





echo 'echo "hello"' > hello.sh
chmod u+x hello.sh
ls -l hello.sh
./hello.sh







QE3.1 Create a text file notes.txt with a few lines of content. Compress it with gzip, peek at the compressed content with zcat, then restore the original with gunzip.







Hint





gzip file replaces file with file.gz. zcat file.gz streams the decompressed content to stdout without touching the file on disk. gunzip file.gz undoes the compression.









Solution





printf "line one\nline two\nline three\n" > notes.txt
gzip notes.txt
ls notes.txt.gz
zcat notes.txt.gz
gunzip notes.txt.gz
cat notes.txt




QE3.2 Bundle the project/ directory from QE1.1 into a single gzipped tar archive called project.tar.gz, list the contents of the archive without extracting, then extract it into a fresh directory restored/.







Hint





Remember the tar flags: create, extract, t = list, z = gzip, verbose, f = file. -C <dir> tells tar to change into <dir> before extracting.









Solution





tar -czvf project.tar.gz project/
tar -tzvf project.tar.gz
mkdir -p restored
tar -xzvf project.tar.gz -C restored
ls -R restored







QE4.1 Download the file at http://beagle.henlab.org/public/course_bioinformatics_genomeanalysis/emboss_data_extended_v1.zip and save it locally as emboss_extra.zip (i.e. with a name different from the URL’s last segment). Do it once with wget and once with curl.







Hint





wget -O <name> <url> writes to a chosen filename. With curl the equivalent is curl -o <name> <url> (lower-case o); curl -O <url> would keep the URL’s filename.









Solution





wget -O emboss_extra.zip http://beagle.henlab.org/public/course_bioinformatics_genomeanalysis/emboss_data_extended_v1.zip

# or, equivalently:
curl -o emboss_extra.zip http://beagle.henlab.org/public/course_bioinformatics_genomeanalysis/emboss_data_extended_v1.zip




QE4.2 You have a local file results.txt you want to send to your home directory on HPC2N (username@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se). Write the scp command to upload it, and the rsync command that would do the same job but only re-transfer changed files if you run it again.







Hint





scp <src> <user>@<host>:<dst> copies a single file. rsync -avz <src> <user>@<host>:<dst> is the recommended workhorse: archive mode, verbose, zipped over the wire, and it only re-sends what has changed. Replace username with your actual HPC2N login.









Solution





# one-shot copy
scp results.txt username@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se:~/

# resumable / incremental copy
rsync -avz results.txt username@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se:~/
To pull a file the other way, swap the arguments: scp username@kebnekaise.hpc2n.umu.se:~/results.txt .







QE5.1 Download the FASTQ file at https://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/fastq/SRR390/SRR390728/SRR390728_1.fastq.gz (a small public run from ENA) using wget, then without uncompressing it on disk, count how many reads it contains. Recall that each read in a FASTQ takes exactly 4 lines.







Hint






zcat file.fastq.gz streams the decompressed content. Pipe into wc -l to count lines.
Divide the line count by 4 — or have the shell do it for you with $(( … / 4 )).










Hint





If the download is slow or blocked, any small .fastq.gz you already have on disk works just as well — the line-count trick is the same.









Solution





wget https://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/fastq/SRR390/SRR390728/SRR390728_1.fastq.gz

lines=$(zcat SRR390728_1.fastq.gz | wc -l)
echo "lines = $lines"
echo "reads = $(( lines / 4 ))"

title: 4.2 Simulations and bootstrapping
text:
Sometimes the math just becomes too difficult, and it is better to let the computer figure things out. In this lesson, we will look at how simulations given a mathematical model can be used to analyse its behaviour. In particular, when the model has an element of randomness, we can look at the distributions of properties over repeated simulations — which in statistics is called “bootstrapping”. The integrals required for Bayesian statistics (next module) are actually solved using a type of bootstrap (Markov chain Monte Carlo), but here we will restrict ourselves to much simpler and more general cases.
We included bootstrapping in this course simply because it is such a Swiss army knife in bioinformatics. It’s easy to implement, and thus ubiquitous!
Study advice: The rest of module 4 does not depend on this submodule. If you get stuck, or are short on time, you can come back and finish it later.

title: 4.2 Simulations and bootstrapping
text:
Computationally intensive methods, and bootstrap
Introduction: See this video that introduces the concept (Canvas/Kaltura: 5_5 Bootstrap; please ignore the video numbering).
Use basic bootstrap to prove the central limit theorem:
The central limit theorem states that the average of N i.i.d. variables having variance \(\sigma^2\) converges toward a normal distribution with variance \(\sigma^2 / N\). With bootstrap we can show also what a complex distribution it can have for small N!

Take inspiration from bootstrap_basics.R (in bootstrap_and_sim.zip).
As for the number of bootstraps, just keep it “somewhat high”. The higher it is, the more precise is your answer. Motivating the number of bootstraps is beyond this course. In practice, the number is picked based on experience. By running the same bootstrap multiple times, you can assess if the precision appears “good enough” for your problem. Tricks to increase precision include parametric bootstrapping, and bias correction. Again, both of these are outside this course, but see Deep reading at the end of this module.
Q1.1. Plot the distribution of the mean for several different N; get an intuition for what is going on.







Hint





For each N, draw N samples from your base distribution, take the mean, and repeat many times. replicate() is your friend.









Hint





Use hist() (or ggplot) on the vector of means. Try N <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50) and use par(mfrow=c(2,3)) to see them side by side.









Solution






nboot <- 10000
Ns <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (N in Ns) {
  means <- replicate(nboot, mean(runif(N)))  # base dist = Uniform(0,1)
  hist(means, breaks = 40, main = paste("N =", N), xlab = "sample mean")
}
# As N grows the histogram narrows and looks more Gaussian — the CLT in action.





Q1.2. Change the distribution of the samples to be Poisson(5). What does the distribution of the mean look like?







Hint





Swap runif(N) for rpois(N, lambda = 5). Everything else stays the same.









Solution






nboot <- 10000
Ns <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (N in Ns) {
  means <- replicate(nboot, mean(rpois(N, lambda = 5)))
  hist(means, breaks = 40, main = paste("N =", N), xlab = "sample mean")
}
# For N=1 you see the discrete Poisson; as N grows it becomes a smooth bell
# centred at 5 with variance 5/N — exactly what the CLT predicts.





Q1.3. Optional: Make the distribution of the samples a Gaussian mixture model and see how it affects things.

GMMs are also used for unsupervised clustering. If you are interested, see for example this video for an introduction to how they can be fitted to data: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=REypj2sy_5U.








Hint





To sample from a GMM: first pick a component (e.g. with sample() according to mixture weights), then draw from that component’s rnorm().









Hint





A two-component mixture with well-separated means gives a clearly bimodal base distribution — but the mean-of-N still converges to a single Gaussian.









Solution






rgmm <- function(n, mus = c(-3, 3), sds = c(1, 1), w = c(0.5, 0.5)) {
  k <- sample(seq_along(mus), n, replace = TRUE, prob = w)
  rnorm(n, mean = mus[k], sd = sds[k])
}

nboot <- 10000
Ns <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (N in Ns) {
  means <- replicate(nboot, mean(rgmm(N)))
  hist(means, breaks = 40, main = paste("N =", N), xlab = "sample mean")
}
# N=1: clearly bimodal. As N grows the bimodality vanishes and a single
# Gaussian emerges around the overall mean. The CLT works even for ugly
# base distributions, as long as the variance is finite.

title: 4.2 Simulations and bootstrapping
text:
Simulations, with and without bootstrap
Introduction: See this video which illustrates how simulations can be performed, and bootstrapping added on top to find the average properties of random processes (Canvas/Kaltura: 5_5 Simulations).
Use bootstrap over a simulation of a birth-death process:

The example code is in birth_death.R (in bootstrap_and_sim.zip).
Q2.1 Very optional, if you like math. If X ~ Poisson(a) and Y ~ Poisson(b), show that X+Y ~ Poisson(a+b).







Hint





This is mainly a brute-force exercise in computing sums. Use that X and Y are positive variables, and thus the sum is finite.









Hint





Write \(P(X+Y=n)\) as a convolution \(\sum_{k=0}^{n} P(X=k)\,P(Y=n-k)\). Pull out \(e^{-(a+b)}/n!\) and recognise the binomial theorem inside.









Solution





Using independence and the convolution formula, \[
P(X+Y=n) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} P(X=k)\,P(Y=n-k)
        = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{a^{k} e^{-a}}{k!}\,\frac{b^{n-k} e^{-b}}{(n-k)!}.
\] Factor out the constants and multiply by \(n!/n!\): \[
= \frac{e^{-(a+b)}}{n!} \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}\, a^{k}\, b^{n-k}.
\] By the binomial theorem the sum equals \((a+b)^n\), so \[
P(X+Y=n) = \frac{(a+b)^{n} e^{-(a+b)}}{n!},
\] which is exactly the pmf of \(\text{Poisson}(a+b)\). \(\blacksquare\)




Q2.2 If you start with n=10, and \(\alpha = 0.95\), what is the average time until the population dies out?

To compute the average, wrap all the code in a loop, and run it multiple times. Keep the time of death for each iteration in the loop.








Hint





You do not need to use functions if you prefer not; you can instead opt to wrap all the code inside a plain for-loop.









Hint





In a for-loop, you can keep adding values to a list as follows: mylist <- c(); for (...) { ...... mylist <- c(mylist, new_value) }









Solution






alpha <- 0.95
n0    <- 10
nboot <- 2000

times_of_death <- c()
for (b in 1:nboot) {
  n <- n0
  t <- 0
  while (n > 0) {
    n <- rbinom(1, n, alpha)   # each individual survives with prob alpha
    t <- t + 1
  }
  times_of_death <- c(times_of_death, t)
}

mean(times_of_death)
# Roughly ~65 timesteps for n0=10, alpha=0.95 (exact value varies with seed).





Q2.3 If you start with n=10, and \(\alpha = 0.95\), what is the standard deviation of the time until death?







Hint





Reuse the times_of_death vector from Q2.2 and call sd().









Solution






sd(times_of_death)
# Typically around 18-20 timesteps — the distribution is fairly broad and right-skewed.
hist(times_of_death, breaks = 40)





Q2.4 Optional: A measure of relative variance is std(t) / mean(t); qualitatively, how does this depend on n?

bonus: Generate a plot showing the trend.








Hint





Wrap Q2.2 in an outer loop over starting populations n0. Save mean and sd for each.









Hint





The ratio sd/mean decreases as n0 grows — larger starting populations have more deterministic crash times (relatively speaking).









Solution






alpha <- 0.95
nboot <- 1000
n0s   <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200)

ratios <- sapply(n0s, function(n0) {
  ts <- replicate(nboot, {
    n <- n0; t <- 0
    while (n > 0) { n <- rbinom(1, n, alpha); t <- t + 1 }
    t
  })
  sd(ts) / mean(ts)
})

plot(n0s, ratios, type = "b", log = "x",
     xlab = "starting n", ylab = "sd(t) / mean(t)")
# Ratio shrinks with n — relative noise drops, consistent with a 1/sqrt(n)-ish trend.





Q2.5 Optional: The average follows a normal distribution, with the induced variance \(\sigma^2 / n\); how many bootstraps need you generate to get the variance of mean time to population crash within ±1 individual, with 95% confidence interval? (This is a bit more mathy; if you know \(\sigma\) then qnorm() and some math can give you n.)







Hint





A 95% CI for the mean has half-width \(1.96 \cdot \sigma / \sqrt{n}\). Set this equal to 1 and solve for \(n\).









Solution





We require \(1.96 \cdot \sigma / \sqrt{n} \le 1\), i.e. \(n \ge (1.96\,\sigma)^2\).

sigma <- sd(times_of_death)         # from Q2.3, e.g. ~19
n_needed <- ceiling((qnorm(0.975) * sigma)^2)
n_needed
# With sigma ~= 19 this gives n_needed ~= 1400 bootstraps.




Practice simulation of the discrete time and finite population Lotka–Volterra model in R:
Optional: You can do some background reading about the original Lotka–Volterra equations on Wikipedia.

Start with the prewritten script lotka_volterra.R (in bootstrap_and_sim.zip).
Q3.1 Currently it plots prey vs time, and predators vs time; plot instead prey vs predators, what is also called the phase space of the state in which the system can be in.







Hint





Replace the two time-series plots with a single plot(prey, predators, type = "l"). The trajectory should curl around an attractor.









Solution






# After running the simulation loop from lotka_volterra.R:
plot(prey, predators, type = "l",
     xlab = "prey", ylab = "predators",
     main = "Phase space")
points(prey[1], predators[1], pch = 19, col = "green")   # start
points(tail(prey,1), tail(predators,1), pch = 19, col = "red")  # end





Q3.2 Play with the parameters. For how long can you make it cycle? What seems to make the population crash? (no single correct answer)







Hint





Try lowering predator efficiency or increasing prey reproduction — cycles widen. Crashes tend to happen when a population dips below ~1 and rounding/randomness kills the last individual.









Solution





There is no single correct answer. Typical observations:

Small finite populations crash quickly because Poisson/binomial noise can wipe out predators or prey when their count is low.
Very aggressive predation (high attack rate) overshoots the prey and then predators starve.
Balanced parameters with larger starting populations can cycle for thousands of timesteps before noise eventually causes a crash.


# Example: try a parameter sweep, looking at survival time
# (see Q3.3 for the wrapped function).





Q3.3 Wrap the simulation in a function so you can bootstrap it.







Hint





Make the parameters (n_prey0, n_pred0, the rates, tmax) function arguments. Return a data frame or list with the trajectories and the time-of-crash.









Solution






simulate_lv <- function(n_prey0 = 100, n_pred0 = 20,
                        a = 0.1, b = 0.005,
                        c = 0.005, d = 0.05,
                        tmax = 2000) {
  prey      <- numeric(tmax); prey[1]      <- n_prey0
  predators <- numeric(tmax); predators[1] <- n_pred0
  t_crash   <- NA
  for (t in 2:tmax) {
    # ... whatever update rule lotka_volterra.R uses,
    # written in terms of the function arguments above.
    if (prey[t] <= 0 || predators[t] <= 0) { t_crash <- t; break }
  }
  list(prey = prey, predators = predators, t_crash = t_crash)
}





Q3.4 What is the average time until all prey are eaten?







Hint





Call simulate_lv() many times with replicate(), pull out t_crash, and take mean(). Treat runs that survive to tmax carefully — either bump up tmax or exclude them.









Solution






nboot <- 500
ts <- replicate(nboot, simulate_lv()$t_crash)
mean(ts, na.rm = TRUE)
# The exact value depends entirely on the parameters chosen.





Q3.5 What is the variance in time? Is the distribution symmetric?







Hint





var(ts) and sd(ts); check symmetry visually with hist(ts) and compare mean(ts) to median(ts).









Solution






var(ts, na.rm = TRUE)
sd(ts,  na.rm = TRUE)
hist(ts, breaks = 40)
abline(v = mean(ts, na.rm = TRUE), col = "red")
abline(v = median(ts, na.rm = TRUE), col = "blue")
# Typically right-skewed: many runs crash relatively early, with a long tail
# of "lucky" runs that cycle for a long time. mean > median.





Q3.6 Assuming the model can run for eternity (simply ignore any samples after it crashes), what is the average number of prey?







Hint





For each run, take prey[1:t_crash-1] (the pre-crash trajectory) and average those. Then average across runs.









Hint





Equivalently: pool all pre-crash prey counts from all bootstrap runs into one big vector and take the mean.









Solution






nboot <- 500
all_prey <- c()
for (b in 1:nboot) {
  sim <- simulate_lv()
  tc  <- if (is.na(sim$t_crash)) length(sim$prey) else sim$t_crash - 1
  all_prey <- c(all_prey, sim$prey[1:tc])
}
mean(all_prey)
# This is the long-run time-average prey population, conditional on survival.

title: 4.2 Simulations and bootstrapping
text:
Deep reading
This is “the” book on bootstrapping: https://www.hms.harvard.edu/bss/neuro/bornlab/nb204/statistics/bootstrap.pdf

title: 4.2 Simulations and bootstrapping
text:
Extra exercise material
A second pass at the same material, for extra practice. Same conventions as above — try each question first, then peek.

Bootstrap of the mean (extra)

QE1.1 Repeat the CLT demo with an exponential base distribution, rexp(N, rate = 1). The exponential is strongly right-skewed — at what N does the distribution of the mean start to look Gaussian?







Hint





Same template as Q1.1: replicate(nboot, mean(rexp(N, rate = 1))). Loop over a few values of N and hist() each.









Hint





The theoretical mean is 1/rate = 1 and variance is 1/rate^2 = 1, so the distribution of the mean should be centred on 1 with variance 1/N. Skew is still visible at N=5 but mostly gone by N=30 or so.









Solution






nboot <- 10000
Ns <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 100)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (N in Ns) {
  means <- replicate(nboot, mean(rexp(N, rate = 1)))
  hist(means, breaks = 40, main = paste("N =", N), xlab = "sample mean")
}
# Heavy right-skew at small N gradually symmetrises; by N~30 it is visually
# indistinguishable from a Gaussian centred at 1 with sd ~ 1/sqrt(N).





QE1.2 Try a log-normal base distribution, rlnorm(N, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1). How does the convergence speed compare to the exponential?







Hint





Log-normal is even more skewed than exponential — its tail is heavier. Expect to need larger N before the mean looks Gaussian.









Solution






nboot <- 10000
Ns <- c(1, 5, 30, 100, 300, 1000)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (N in Ns) {
  means <- replicate(nboot, mean(rlnorm(N, meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1)))
  hist(means, breaks = 40, main = paste("N =", N), xlab = "sample mean")
}
# Convergence is slower than for the exponential: even at N=100 there is
# visible right-skew. The CLT still works, but heavy tails slow it down.





QE1.3 Now try the Cauchy distribution, rcauchy(N). The CLT fails here — generate the distribution of the mean for increasing N and explain in prose what goes wrong.







Hint





The Cauchy has undefined mean and infinite variance — the assumptions of the CLT are violated.









Hint





In fact, the mean of N Cauchy samples is itself Cauchy-distributed (with the same scale). So averaging does not help at all.









Solution






nboot <- 10000
Ns <- c(1, 10, 100, 1000)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
for (N in Ns) {
  means <- replicate(nboot, mean(rcauchy(N)))
  hist(means, breaks = 100, main = paste("N =", N),
       xlab = "sample mean", xlim = c(-20, 20))
}

Prose: The CLT requires the base distribution to have finite variance. The Cauchy has no defined mean and infinite variance, so the theorem does not apply. Empirically: the distribution of mean(rcauchy(N)) does not narrow as N grows — it stays Cauchy-distributed with the same scale parameter. The “law of large numbers” also fails: the sample mean does not converge to any fixed value. This is the canonical cautionary example for heavy-tailed data in biology (e.g. some gene-expression and network-degree distributions).

# Quick sanity check: sample variance of the mean does not shrink with N.
set.seed(1)
var(replicate(2000, mean(rcauchy(10))))

[1] 3543.705

var(replicate(2000, mean(rcauchy(1000))))

[1] 7279.409

# Both are large and erratic — no 1/N scaling.






Birth-death (extra)

QE2.1 Run the birth-death simulation with n0 = 10 and alpha = 0.99 (a much more “stable” population). Estimate the probability that the population survives past T = 500 timesteps.







Hint





For each bootstrap iteration, run the simulation up to T timesteps and record whether n > 0 at the end. The empirical survival probability is just the mean of that 0/1 vector.









Solution






alpha <- 0.99
n0    <- 10
T     <- 500
nboot <- 2000

survived <- replicate(nboot, {
  n <- n0
  for (t in 1:T) {
    n <- rbinom(1, n, alpha)
    if (n == 0) break
  }
  n > 0
})

mean(survived)   # empirical P(survive past T)
# With alpha=0.99 and n0=10 a sizeable fraction makes it past 500 steps,
# but many runs still die out — the exact figure depends on the seed.





QE2.2 Vary the initial population n0 over a range (e.g. c(2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100)) at fixed alpha = 0.95. Plot mean time-of-death against n0. Is the relationship linear, logarithmic, or something else?







Hint





Wrap the inner simulation in replicate(), sweep n0, and plot(n0s, mean_t). Try both linear and log axes.









Hint





Mean time-to-extinction grows roughly logarithmically in n0 for a Galton-Watson-like process at fixed per-individual survival.









Solution






alpha <- 0.95
nboot <- 1000
n0s   <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500)

mean_t <- sapply(n0s, function(n0) {
  ts <- replicate(nboot, {
    n <- n0; t <- 0
    while (n > 0) { n <- rbinom(1, n, alpha); t <- t + 1 }
    t
  })
  mean(ts)
})

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(n0s, mean_t, type = "b", xlab = "n0", ylab = "mean time of death")
plot(n0s, mean_t, type = "b", log = "x",
     xlab = "n0 (log)", ylab = "mean time of death")
# The right-hand log-x plot is roughly linear: mean death time ~ log(n0).





QE2.3 Optional: For alpha = 0.95, estimate the median and interquartile range of the time-of-death starting from n0 = 10. Compare to the mean and sd from Q2.2/Q2.3. Why might the median be a more honest summary?







Hint





median() and quantile(x, c(0.25, 0.75)). The distribution is right-skewed, so the mean is pulled up by the long tail.









Solution






alpha <- 0.95
n0    <- 10
nboot <- 2000
ts <- replicate(nboot, {
  n <- n0; t <- 0
  while (n > 0) { n <- rbinom(1, n, alpha); t <- t + 1 }
  t
})
mean(ts);   median(ts)
sd(ts);     IQR(ts)
quantile(ts, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75))
# Median < mean because of the right-skewed tail of "lucky" long-lived runs.
# The IQR is a more robust spread measure than sd for skewed data.






Lotka-Volterra and other simulations (extra)

QE3.1 Sensitivity analysis. Using simulate_lv() from Q3.3, vary the predator death rate gamma over c(0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.12, 0.2) while keeping all other parameters fixed. For each value, estimate mean time-to-crash from nboot = 200 runs. Which gamma lets the system survive longest?







Hint





Wrap replicate(nboot, simulate_lv(gamma = g)$t_crash) in sapply() over the gamma vector.









Hint





Very low gamma → predators never die, eat all prey, then starve. Very high gamma → predators crash on their own. There is a sweet spot in between.









Solution






gammas <- c(0.02, 0.05, 0.08, 0.12, 0.2)
nboot  <- 200
mean_tc <- sapply(gammas, function(g) {
  ts <- replicate(nboot, simulate_lv(gamma = g)$t_crash)
  mean(ts, na.rm = TRUE)
})
plot(gammas, mean_tc, type = "b",
     xlab = "predator death rate gamma",
     ylab = "mean time to crash")
# Expect a non-monotonic curve with a peak at the balanced value.





QE3.2 Find (by manual sweep) a parameter region that produces sustained oscillations — say, the system survives past tmax = 5000 for at least 80% of bootstrap runs. Report the parameters and the empirical survival fraction.







Hint





Larger starting populations and gentler rates are more forgiving of stochastic noise. Try n_prey0 = 500, n_pred0 = 100, mild a, b, c, d.









Solution






nboot <- 200
res <- replicate(nboot, simulate_lv(
  n_prey0 = 500, n_pred0 = 100,
  a = 0.1, b = 0.001, c = 0.001, d = 0.05,
  tmax = 5000
)$t_crash)
mean(is.na(res))   # fraction that survived to tmax
# Tune the rates until this fraction is >= 0.8.





QE3.3 Estimate the average period of the prey-predator oscillation in phase space for one long surviving run. (Use any reasonable definition, e.g. consecutive maxima of the prey trajectory.)







Hint





A simple way: find local maxima of prey with which(diff(sign(diff(prey))) == -2) + 1, then take diff() of those indices and average.









Solution






sim <- simulate_lv(n_prey0 = 500, n_pred0 = 100,
                   a = 0.1, b = 0.001, c = 0.001, d = 0.05,
                   tmax = 5000)
prey <- sim$prey
# Smooth a little so noise does not create spurious local maxima
prey_s <- stats::filter(prey, rep(1/21, 21), sides = 2)
peaks  <- which(diff(sign(diff(prey_s))) == -2) + 1
periods <- diff(peaks)
mean(periods); sd(periods)
# Period depends on parameters; the classical continuous LV has period
# ~ 2*pi/sqrt(a*c) in the linearised regime around equilibrium.






Bonus: SIR and HWE

QE4.1 Run sir_basic.R from the zip. Compute the peak infected fraction (max(I) / popsize) and the day at which the peak occurs. Bootstrap it: wrap the simulation in a function and run it nboot = 200 times — what is the distribution of the peak fraction?







Hint





Copy the body of sir_basic.R into a function simulate_sir(beta = 0.1, gamma = 0.1, popsize = 20, ndays = 50) returning the per-day SIR counts. Compute max(I)/popsize from each run.









Solution






simulate_sir <- function(beta = 0.1, gamma = 0.1,
                        popsize = 20, ndays = 50) {
  indiv <- data.frame(num = 1:popsize, state = "S")
  indiv$state[1] <- "I"
  log_SIR <- matrix(0, nrow = ndays, ncol = 3,
                    dimnames = list(NULL, c("S","I","R")))
  for (d in 1:ndays) {
    log_SIR[d, ] <- c(sum(indiv$state == "S"),
                      sum(indiv$state == "I"),
                      sum(indiv$state == "R"))
    next_indiv <- indiv
    rate <- sum(indiv$state == "I") * beta
    next_indiv$state[indiv$state == "S" &
                     runif(nrow(indiv)) < rate] <- "I"
    next_indiv$state[indiv$state == "I" &
                     runif(nrow(indiv)) < gamma] <- "R"
    indiv <- next_indiv
  }
  log_SIR
}

nboot <- 200
peaks <- replicate(nboot, {
  m <- simulate_sir()
  max(m[, "I"]) / 20
})
hist(peaks, breaks = 30, xlab = "peak infected fraction")
mean(peaks); sd(peaks)
# Highly variable for popsize = 20 — many epidemics fizzle out, a few explode.





QE4.2 Optional: Complete the hwe.R script (fill in the #TODO lines so each child draws one allele uniformly at random from each parent). Run it for 50 generations starting from half AA and half aa, and check that genotype frequencies stabilise near the Hardy–Weinberg expectation \(p^2 : 2pq : q^2\) with \(p = q = 0.5\) (i.e. 25% AA, 50% Aa, 25% aa).







Hint





sample(c(parent$allele1, parent$allele2), 1) picks one of the two parental alleles uniformly.









Hint





After completing the loop, plot log_num$num_AA / popsize, num_Aa / popsize, num_aa / popsize over generations and compare to 0.25, 0.50, 0.25.









Solution






popsize <- 200   # bump up so HWE is visible above drift noise
indiv <- data.frame(num = 1:popsize, allele1 = "A", allele2 = "A",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
indiv$allele1[(popsize/2 + 1):popsize] <- "a"
indiv$allele2[(popsize/2 + 1):popsize] <- "a"

log_num <- NULL
for (gen in 1:50) {
  log_num <- rbind(log_num, data.frame(
    num_AA = sum(indiv$allele1 == "A" & indiv$allele2 == "A"),
    num_aa = sum(indiv$allele1 == "a" & indiv$allele2 == "a"),
    num_Aa = sum(indiv$allele1 != indiv$allele2)
  ))
  p1 <- sample(1:popsize, popsize, replace = TRUE)
  p2 <- sample(1:popsize, popsize, replace = TRUE)
  next_indiv <- data.frame(allele1 = NA, allele2 = NA)
  for (i in 1:popsize) {
    a1 <- sample(c(indiv$allele1[p1[i]], indiv$allele2[p1[i]]), 1)
    a2 <- sample(c(indiv$allele1[p2[i]], indiv$allele2[p2[i]]), 1)
    next_indiv[i, ] <- c(a1, a2)
  }
  indiv <- next_indiv
}

tail(log_num / popsize)
# After a few generations: ~0.25 AA, ~0.50 Aa, ~0.25 aa,
# matching Hardy-Weinberg with p = q = 0.5 (modulo drift).

title: 4.4 RNA-seq analysis
text: In this module we will finally perform an RNA-seq analysis, putting previous modules into action!

title: 4.4 RNA-seq analysis
text:
From FASTQ to count matrix
Learn first how to align raw sequencing data, and produce a count matrix: The count matrix represents RNA molecule counts, and is obtained after aligning sequencing data, and comparing with the reference gene annotation. We will explain how to get this count matrix the common way, but also an incredibly fast shortcut to it using linear algebra (Canvas/Kaltura video: 4_5_alignment_for_rnaseq v2).

As mentioned, salmon is a pseudocount tool, going from FASTQ to count matrix directly. You can read more here: https://combine-lab.github.io/salmon/about
Salmon guide

Get Salmon for pseudocounting:

if you use HPC2N, you can load it through:
ml load GCC/13.2.0 Salmon/1.10.3
If you run on your own computer, you can install it through conda.

Check that it runs by simply typing salmon in the terminal. You should get a help page.
Index a genome
Building a genome the scale of the human genome can take hours. Thus, for this course, we have already prepared a ready-made index; or rather, we found ready-made indices at http://refgenomes.databio.org, luckily also for human/salmon.
You can use the following code to create a directory and download an index. Be sure to put it in a directory to avoid files all over your account!
mkdir salmon_human_index
cd salmon_human_index

If you want to try building your own (optional), check the Salmon guide. It boils down to:

Downloading the human reference genome, and it has to be the cDNA for each gene (or CDS, coding sequence). To find suitable files, you would normally start digging here, and at some point you will land here. Whatever you do, ensure to use the gene cDNA FASTA and not the chromosomal DNA! (BWA/STAR would want the latter instead.)
Running salmon index -t ... -i .... Use multiple CPUs to speed up the process.

Get FASTQ with RNA to quantify:
Let’s investigate some neuroblastoma! In a dataset, it has been treated with a drug. We will compare with untreated cells. The data is from a previous study: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/ArrayExpress/studies/E-MTAB-9315?query=E-MTAB-9315
There is plenty of public data that you can reanalyze and make new findings. Also to get new ideas or help design experiments. This saves a lot of time in the lab!
You will find a link to ENA with raw FASTQ files. You need at least 2 treated and 2 untreated samples for the statistics — it is kept to a minimum to reduce compute time for this course; ideally you would want 3-5 replicates each.
To save you time, we have picked suitable files to download. Here are the commands:
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4319001/RUN466-6-26081-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq1BR_S3_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4319005/RUN466-20-26210-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq5BR_S12_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4318985/RUN466-5-26079-CLBGA-DMSO-75-Celasterol-RNAseq1BR_S4_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4318989/RUN466-9-26102-CLBGA-DMSO-75-Celasterol-RNAseq2BR_S13_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz

Q1.1 Download the required raw files.







Hint





Run the four wget commands listed above in a directory where you want to keep the FASTQ files.









Solution





wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4319001/RUN466-6-26081-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq1BR_S3_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4319005/RUN466-20-26210-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq5BR_S12_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4318985/RUN466-5-26079-CLBGA-DMSO-75-Celasterol-RNAseq1BR_S4_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz
wget -nc ftp://ftp.sra.ebi.ac.uk/vol1/run/ERR431/ERR4318989/RUN466-9-26102-CLBGA-DMSO-75-Celasterol-RNAseq2BR_S13_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz



Quantify the number RNA molecules per gene:
Using the index you downloaded, stored in directory salmon_human_index, you can estimate the number of RNA molecules for each gene using this command:
salmon quant -i salmon_human_index -l A \
    -r RUN466-20-26210-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq5BR_S12_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz \
    -p 1 --validateMappings -o quants/IC50_5_quant
Here -p 1 means to use one CPU. You can arrange to use multiple if you want. The output is specified using -o.






Note



You can put \ at the end of any bash command lines if you want to manually divide them up to increase readability. But be careful when copying above as there cannot be any newlines when you paste it in (bash will then think that you are giving it 3 separate commands, and fail).



Q1.2: Quantify each of the 4 FASTQ-files you downloaded. Give them suitable simple names. Note that the subdirectory salmon_human_index must be in the directory you are running the command in (or you need to adjust the command).







Hint





Run the same salmon quant command four times, once per FASTQ, changing both -r and -o for each sample. Pick short names like IC50_1, IC50_5, DMSO_1, DMSO_2.









Solution





salmon quant -i salmon_human_index -l A \
    -r RUN466-6-26081-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq1BR_S3_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz \
    -p 1 --validateMappings -o quants/IC50_1_quant

salmon quant -i salmon_human_index -l A \
    -r RUN466-20-26210-CLBGA-IC50-Celasterol-RNAseq5BR_S12_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz \
    -p 1 --validateMappings -o quants/IC50_5_quant

salmon quant -i salmon_human_index -l A \
    -r RUN466-5-26079-CLBGA-DMSO-75-Celasterol-RNAseq1BR_S4_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz \
    -p 1 --validateMappings -o quants/DMSO_1_quant

salmon quant -i salmon_human_index -l A \
    -r RUN466-9-26102-CLBGA-DMSO-75-Celasterol-RNAseq2BR_S13_L001_R1_001.fastq.gz \
    -p 1 --validateMappings -o quants/DMSO_2_quant



Load the counts in R:
As is common, data is not always stored in the simplest format. We have written some code here to enable you to read the counts for each library into one matrix in R. It assumes that you stored all outputs in the directory ~/glio/quants/.
## Read each separate salmon output of counts
all_counts <- list()
rootdir <- "~/glio/quants/"
for (f in list.files(rootdir)) {
  print(f)
  onedat <- read.csv(file.path(rootdir, f, "quant.sf"), sep = "\t")[, c("Name", "NumReads")]
  onedat$f <- f
  all_counts[[f]] <- onedat
}
## Put into one single count matrix
cnt <- reshape2::acast(do.call(rbind, all_counts), Name ~ f, value.var = "NumReads")

Q1.3: You can already check which genes have the most amount of RNA. Which transcript has the most RNA?







Hint





You can, e.g., use the commands order and sort to get the list in a suitable order.









Hint





Compute the row sums of the count matrix and order the rows by those sums in decreasing order.









Solution






cnt[order(rowSums(cnt), decreasing = TRUE), ][1:10, ]

The top transcript is typically ENST00000387347 (MT-RNR2 / mitochondrial 16S rRNA) — mitochondrial transcripts dominate in most bulk RNA-seq libraries.




Q1.4: Optional: Are there any genes you recognize? You can look up any geneID such as on Ensembl. Here is the page for the human gene IL4.







Hint





Paste an ENST... ID into the Ensembl search box. The very top hits are usually mitochondrial RNAs, ribosomal RNAs, or common housekeeping genes (GAPDH, ACTB, etc.).









Solution





The most abundant transcripts in bulk RNA-seq are usually mitochondrial (MT-RNR1, MT-RNR2, MT-CO1…) and housekeeping genes such as ACTB, GAPDH, and ribosomal protein genes (RPL/RPS family). These are highly expressed in essentially every human cell type.

title: 4.4 RNA-seq analysis
text:
Differential expression analysis
See this video, showing the overall workflow from counts to statistical test (Canvas/Kaltura: 4.3 deseq).

Model matrices are central to analysis of RNA-seq, microarray, proteomic and what-have-you data. Once you grasp this concept, you can do most bioinformatics statistical analysis!
You will see that you can model a simple comparison between condition A and B (for two samples) as
\[
  \begin{bmatrix} \text{counts}_A \\ \text{counts}_B \end{bmatrix}
  \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(
  \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} \text{baseline} \\ \text{treatment} \end{bmatrix}
  \right)
  \]
and then just compute \(P(\text{baseline}_2 < q)\).

The model matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(P(\text{treatment} < q)\) is being evaluated to see if the expression is different from 0.
We call \(\text{treatment}\) a contrast.

Alternatively, equivalently,
\[
  \begin{bmatrix} \text{counts}_A \\ \text{counts}_B \end{bmatrix}
  \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\!\left(
  \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}
  \begin{bmatrix} \text{baseline}_1 \\ \text{baseline}_2 \end{bmatrix}
  \right)
  \]
but the test becomes a bit more complicated instead: \(P(\text{baseline}_2 - \text{baseline}_1 < q)\).

The model matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\).
\(P(\text{baseline}_2 - \text{baseline}_1 < q)\) is evaluated to see if it is different from 0.
\(\text{baseline}_2 - \text{baseline}_1\) is the contrast in this case.

The Poisson distribution we looked at only models the sequencing process. To also account for biological variation, we will instead use the negative binomial distribution, which turns out to be a natural extension. Optional reading at Wikipedia.
Optional reading on the origin of the negative binomial distribution, but even better is the DESeq2 paper.

Differential expression theory:

Q2.1: Using pen and paper, convince yourself that log(fold change) = 0 means that there is no change.







Hint





What value of \(x\) gives \(\log(x) = 0\)? And what does that value of the fold change \(x = \text{new}/\text{old}\) mean?









Solution





\(\log(x) = 0 \iff x = 1\). A fold change of \(1 = \text{new}/\text{old}\) means \(\text{new} = \text{old}\), i.e. no change in expression.




Q2.2: Using pen and paper, convince yourself that high −log(p-value) means smaller p-values, and thus higher significance.







Hint





\(\log\) is monotonically increasing, so as \(p\) decreases, \(\log(p)\) decreases, and \(-\log(p)\) increases.









Solution





For \(p \in (0, 1]\), \(\log(p) \le 0\), so \(-\log(p) \ge 0\). As \(p \to 0\), \(-\log(p) \to \infty\). Thus a high \(-\log_{10}(p)\) on the y-axis corresponds to a tiny p-value, i.e. a more significant result.



Set up the condition data frame:
To run DESeq2 or any similar package, you need a data frame with information about the samples. The row names should correspond to sample names (i.e. column names in the count matrix). If you don’t have a condition data frame, you can often create it from the names of the samples. This is a starting point:
cond <- data.frame(
  row.names = colnames(cnt)
)
cond$treatment <- ...
You want to obtain a column called treatment, for each sample. In this case, DMSO and IC50 (or anything you prefer that is human-interpretable).

Q2.3: Fill in the column.







Hint





The stringr R package has great functions for string manipulation. str_split_fixed and str_split_i are really useful here.









Hint





The sample (column) names contain DMSO and IC50 as one of the dash-separated tokens. Split on - and pick that token.









Solution






library(stringr)
cond <- data.frame(row.names = colnames(cnt))
cond$treatment <- str_split_i(rownames(cond), "-", 5)
cond




Install DESeq2
See here: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/DESeq2.html
Remember to load it after installation!
Run DESeq2 to fit statistical model:
You are now ready to perform the statistical analysis! The following code, largely taken from the vignette (recommended reading!), sets up a pairwise test.
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = round(cnt),  # salmon output non-integer counts; round to integer to fix
  colData   = cond,
  design    = ~ treatment  # specifies model matrix
)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, c("treatment", "a", "b"))  # set appropriately

Q2.4: Adjust to compare treated and untreated samples.







Hint





The contrast argument to results() is c(factor_name, level_numerator, level_denominator). Here the factor is treatment, the levels are IC50 (treated) and DMSO (control).









Solution






dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = round(cnt),
  colData   = cond,
  design    = ~ treatment
)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, c("treatment", "IC50", "DMSO"))





Q2.5: What does the model matrix look like? Does it make sense as compared to the video explanation? (hint: typical exam material!)







Hint





Try model.matrix(~ treatment, data = cond) in R and inspect the rows and columns.









Hint





Compare what you see against the two model-matrix formulations in the video / above (the \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) vs. \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\) examples). Which one is R using? What does each column represent (intercept vs. treatment effect)?









Solution






model.matrix(~ treatment, data = cond)

With two treatment levels (DMSO and IC50) and the default treatment-coding, R picks the first level (alphabetically: DMSO) as the reference. You get a column of 1s (the intercept = DMSO baseline) plus one column that is 1 for IC50 samples and 0 for DMSO samples. This is the first formulation from the video, \[
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix},
\] where the second column directly encodes the treatment effect (the contrast). The second formulation in the video uses two intercepts (one per group) and you compute the contrast as the difference of the two — equivalent, just parameterised differently.



Extract the differentially expressed genes and make a volcano plot:
The output list of genes (unsorted) will look kind of like below.



Example DESeq2 results table



log2FoldChange is the log2(fold change) and what most are interested in.
padj is multiple-hypothesis-testing-adjusted p-value.
Q2.6: Adjusted p-value — this means adjusted for multiple hypothesis testing. What does this mean? This video explains: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HLzS5wPqWR0







Hint





If you test 20,000 genes at \(p < 0.05\), how many false positives would you expect by chance alone?









Solution





Testing tens of thousands of genes simultaneously means many will appear significant by chance alone (at \(p < 0.05\), about 5% of all tests). The adjusted p-value (DESeq2 uses Benjamini–Hochberg by default) controls the false discovery rate (FDR) — the expected proportion of false positives among the genes called significant. Use padj rather than raw pvalue when picking hits.




Q2.7: Make a volcano plot to aid interpretation. This plot is designed as follows:

x-axis: log2 fold change
y-axis: −log10 adjusted p-value








Hint





This is just using ggplot, nothing new! Convert the DESeq2 result to a data frame and use geom_point.









Solution






library(ggplot2)
ggplot(as.data.frame(res), aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_bw()




 - Q2.8: Which gene has the highest significance? Note that ENST* are human gene transcripts. A gene has multiple transcripts (isoforms). Use Ensembl to look up the name of the gene.






Hint





Order the result table by padj and look at the first row. Then paste the ENST... ID into the Ensembl search box.









Solution






res_df <- as.data.frame(res)
res_df <- res_df[order(res_df$padj), ]
head(res_df, 5)
rownames(res_df)[1]  # top transcript ID, look this up on Ensembl

Take the top ENST... ID and search it at https://www.ensembl.org. The gene symbol shown there (e.g. HSPA1A, HMOX1 or similar stress-response gene) is the answer.



Also note that the most significant gene has not changed much up or down in expression!

Q2.9 Optional: Use ggrepel, https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ggrepel/vignettes/ggrepel.html, to highlight the names of the most differentially expressed genes. This is commonly done in articles, and a good package to know.







Hint





Add a geom_text_repel layer that only receives the top-N rows (e.g. smallest padj) so the plot does not get cluttered.









Solution






library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)

res_df <- as.data.frame(res)
res_df$gene <- rownames(res_df)
top_n <- head(res_df[order(res_df$padj), ], 10)

ggplot(res_df, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(padj))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_text_repel(data = top_n, aes(label = gene)) +
  theme_bw()

title: 4.4 RNA-seq analysis
text:
A more complex RNA-seq dataset
Sometimes you are lucky and counts have already been computed for you. Such is the case for this dataset where they have treated two cell lines with an anti-cancer drug: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/ArrayExpress/studies/E-MTAB-14822

Q3.1 Optional: What are the two cell lines? What cell types do they represent? They are commonly used in research!







Hint





Open the ArrayExpress page linked above and look in the sample/metadata section, or download meta.csv and read its columns.









Solution





The two cell lines are listed in the metadata on the ArrayExpress page (and inside meta.csv). They are well-known cancer cell lines — look up each name (e.g. on Cellosaurus, https://www.cellosaurus.org) to find the tissue / cell type of origin.



Download and load the data

Q3.2 From the dataset link, download meta.csv (the condition data frame) and readCounts.csv.gz.







Hint





The files are listed in the “Files” section of the ArrayExpress page. Right-click and “Save link as”, or wget the URL directly.









Solution





# right-click → save the two files from the ArrayExpress page, or
wget https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/files/E-MTAB-14822/meta.csv
wget https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biostudies/files/E-MTAB-14822/readCounts.csv.gz
No need to gunzip — read.csv reads .gz directly.




Q3.3 Load the data into R. This can frequently be the hardest task as there is little agreement on the precise format of CSV/TSV files!

Note that this time you do not have to construct the condition matrix, but it is already provided. But ensure to set the row names to match the column names of the count matrix. Note that you have to break up the treatment column into time (6h, 24h) and treatment (no treatment, 5h of treatment, 10h of treatment).
When you load the count matrix, be careful that you might get the row names instead as column 1. DESeq will be unhappy. To fix this, either move the values to the rownames, or adjust the parameters to read.csv to avoid this (see the help for read.csv; e.g. row.names can be adjusted).








Hint





read.csv("readCounts.csv.gz", row.names = 1) will use the first column as row names. Check head() and dim() afterwards to confirm rows are genes and columns are samples.









Hint





For the meta file, use stringr::str_split_fixed (or similar) on the original treatment column to break it into two new columns: time and treatment_duration.









Solution






library(stringr)

cnt  <- read.csv("readCounts.csv.gz", row.names = 1)
cond <- read.csv("meta.csv")
rownames(cond) <- cond$sample   # use the sample-name column (whatever it is called)

# Ensure ordering matches the count matrix
cond <- cond[colnames(cnt), ]

# Split the treatment column into two new columns (adjust the separator/index
# to match the actual strings in meta.csv)
parts <- str_split_fixed(cond$treatment, "_", 2)
cond$treatment_duration   <- parts[, 1]
cond$time_since_treatment <- parts[, 2]




Perform DE analysis using DESeq2
There is much more you can compare here, since you got both (1) cell type and (2) time since treatment. We will return to this dataset in Module 5 to perform unsupervised machine learning.
Note that there is metadata that you can ignore, such as the position of the sample on the multiwell plate where the sample was prepared.
You can build a multilinear equation describing the expression of genes as: ~ cell_type + treatment_duration + time_since_treatment.

Q3.4 Does this model make sense? No model is perfect! Are there any assumptions built into the model? (this question has no single correct answer)







Hint





The formula ~ cell_type + treatment_duration + time_since_treatment has no : or * terms. What does that mean about how the three factors are assumed to interact?









Solution





The + form assumes purely additive effects on \(\log\) expression — each factor shifts expression independently of the others. In reality, the response to a drug may very well depend on the cell line (a cell-type × treatment interaction), which this model cannot capture. To allow that, you would add an interaction term such as ~ cell_type * treatment_duration. The model also assumes the replicates are independent samples, that the negative-binomial mean-variance relationship holds, and that no important confounders (e.g. batch / plate position) are missing.




Q3.5 What does the model matrix look like? Note as above that there are multiple model matrices that could be used for this problem. How would you have preferred to construct it?







Hint





Use model.matrix(~ cell_type + treatment_duration + time_since_treatment, data = cond) and inspect the columns: there is an intercept column, then one indicator column per non-reference level of each factor.









Solution






mm <- model.matrix(~ cell_type + treatment_duration + time_since_treatment, data = cond)
head(mm)

The first column is the intercept (the reference cell line / no treatment / earliest time). Each remaining column is an indicator for one non-reference level. With \(k\) levels in a factor you get \(k-1\) columns (treatment contrasts). An alternative is the “no-intercept” parametrisation ~ 0 + cell_type + treatment_duration + time_since_treatment, which gives one column per level — easier to read for some contrasts but you still need to choose contrasts carefully.




Q3.6 Which genes are DE between the cell lines? Optional: If you checked what the cell lines are, do any genes make sense to you? (not trivial)







Hint





Run resultsNames(dds) after DESeq(dds) to see which coefficients are available. Pick the one corresponding to cell line and pass it via name=.









Solution






dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(
  countData = round(cnt),
  colData   = cond,
  design    = ~ cell_type + treatment_duration + time_since_treatment
)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)
res_cell <- results(dds, name = "cell_type_X_vs_Y")  # replace X and Y with the actual level names
head(res_cell[order(res_cell$padj), ])

Lineage-marker genes (e.g. tissue-specific transcription factors of the cell types you identified in Q3.1) often top the list.




Q3.7 Which genes are DE due to the treatment? Optional: Do any genes make sense? (not trivial)







Hint





Same approach as Q3.6 but use the treatment_duration_... coefficient instead. Look at resultsNames(dds) to find the exact string.









Solution






resultsNames(dds)
res_treat <- results(dds, name = "treatment_duration_treated_vs_untreated")  # replace with actual name
head(res_treat[order(res_treat$padj), ])

Drug-response genes (e.g. stress-response, apoptosis or cell-cycle genes depending on the drug’s mechanism) tend to dominate the top of the list.

title: 4.4 RNA-seq analysis
text:
Extra exercise material
A second pass at the same material, for extra practice. Same conventions as above — try each question first, then peek.

Alignment and quantification (extra)

QE1.1 What does the --validateMappings flag do in salmon quant, and why would you usually want it on?







Hint





Pseudoalignment by itself only checks which transcripts a read’s k-mers are compatible with. --validateMappings adds an extra step on top of that.









Solution





--validateMappings enables selective alignment: after the fast k-mer-based mapping step, salmon does a lightweight scoring of each candidate mapping against the transcript sequence (similar in spirit to a Smith–Waterman score). This filters out spurious mappings that happen to share k-mers but do not actually align well, giving more accurate quantification at a small extra CPU cost. It is on by default in newer salmon versions and is the recommended setting.




QE1.2 Why use a pseudoaligner like salmon instead of a full splice-aware aligner like STAR or BWA when all you want is a gene-level count matrix?







Hint





Think about what information you actually use downstream (just NumReads per transcript), and what STAR/BWA spend most of their time computing.









Solution





Full aligners produce a base-resolution BAM with the exact genomic coordinate of every read — useful for variant calling, splice-junction discovery, coverage tracks, etc. For a count matrix you only need to know which transcript a read came from, not where on it. Pseudoalignment skips the per-base alignment and is typically 10–100× faster with comparable quantification accuracy. Trade-off: you cannot reuse the output for SNP calling or coverage plots.




QE1.3 Open one of the quant.sf files salmon produced. What are the columns, and which one did we actually use when we built cnt?







Hint





head quants/IC50_1_quant/quant.sf in bash, or read.csv(..., sep = "\t") in R.









Solution






head(read.csv("quants/IC50_1_quant/quant.sf", sep = "\t"))

Columns are Name (transcript ID), Length, EffectiveLength (length corrected for fragment-size distribution), TPM (transcripts per million — length-normalised), and NumReads (estimated read count, possibly fractional from EM). We used NumReads because DESeq2 wants raw counts, not TPM. TPM is for visualisation / within-sample comparison, not for DE testing.





DESeq2 differential expression (extra)

QE2.1 DESeq2 internally normalises libraries with size factors rather than scaling to TPM. Inspect them and explain what they correct for.







Hint





sizeFactors(dds) after DESeq(dds). Compare them to colSums(counts(dds)).









Solution






sizeFactors(dds)
colSums(counts(dds))

Size factors correct for differences in sequencing depth between libraries, and (because they use the median-of-ratios method, not total counts) they are robust to a handful of very highly expressed genes dominating one library. Each raw count is internally divided by its sample’s size factor before fitting.




QE2.2 Inspect the per-gene dispersion estimates with plotDispEsts(dds). What should the plot look like if the model is behaving well?







Hint





There are three things on the plot: per-gene estimates (black), a fitted trend (red), and shrunken final values (blue).









Solution






plotDispEsts(dds)

You want to see dispersion decreasing with mean expression (highly expressed genes are more reproducible), the red trend line passing through the cloud of black dots, and the blue shrunken estimates pulled toward the red curve — strongest shrinkage for low-count genes where the per-gene estimate is unreliable. Bad signs: trend line clearly off the cloud, or dispersions not decreasing with the mean (suggests outliers or a missing covariate).




QE2.3 Make an MA plot with plotMA(res) and explain the axes. What does a “good” MA plot look like for a treatment-vs-control comparison?







Hint





M and A come from microarray days: M = log-ratio, A = average log-intensity.









Solution






plotMA(res, ylim = c(-5, 5))

x-axis (A) is the mean of normalised counts across all samples (log scale). y-axis (M) is the log2FoldChange. Significant genes (padj < 0.05) are coloured. Expectations: the cloud should be centred on M = 0 (most genes do not change), it should funnel — wider at low mean expression where estimates are noisier, narrower at high mean — and significant points should be the ones farthest from y = 0. A cloud that is shifted off zero suggests a normalisation problem.




QE2.4 Run summary(res) and interpret the output. How many genes go up, how many go down, at the default thresholds?







Hint





summary prints LFC > 0 (up), LFC < 0 (down), outliers, and low-count genes filtered by independent filtering.









Solution






summary(res)

The output lists: total genes tested, the default alpha (FDR threshold, 0.1 unless you set otherwise), number of genes with LFC > 0 (up in numerator vs. denominator) and LFC < 0 (down), how many were flagged as outliers (Cook’s distance) and how many were filtered out by independent filtering of low-count genes (which increases statistical power on the genes that remain). You can tighten this with summary(res, alpha = 0.05).




QE2.5 Pick a stricter cutoff than just padj: keep genes with padj < 0.05 and abs(log2FoldChange) > 1. How many are left?







Hint





log2FoldChange > 1 means at least a 2-fold change. Watch out for NA values in padj from independent filtering.









Solution






res_df <- as.data.frame(res)
sig <- subset(res_df, !is.na(padj) & padj < 0.05 & abs(log2FoldChange) > 1)
nrow(sig)
head(sig[order(sig$padj), ])

abs(log2FoldChange) > 1 corresponds to at least a 2-fold up- or down-regulation. Combining it with padj removes genes that are statistically significant but biologically tiny (common with very deep sequencing — tiny shifts get tiny p-values).





Model matrices and contrasts (extra)

QE2.6 Suppose you want IC50 to be the reference level instead of the default alphabetical pick (DMSO). Use relevel to do this and re-fit. Does the model matrix or the contrast change?







Hint





cond$treatment <- relevel(factor(cond$treatment), ref = "IC50") before constructing dds.









Solution






cond$treatment <- relevel(factor(cond$treatment), ref = "IC50")
dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(round(cnt), cond, ~ treatment)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)  # now "treatment_DMSO_vs_IC50"

The model matrix still has two columns (intercept + one indicator), but the indicator column is now 1 for DMSO samples instead of for IC50 samples. The fitted log-fold change has the opposite sign of before — same biology, different reference. Always check resultsNames(dds) (or the contrast = argument to results()) to know which direction you are looking at.




QE2.7 What does model.matrix(~ 0 + treatment, data = cond) look like (the no-intercept form), and how would you extract the IC50-vs-DMSO contrast from a dds fitted with design = ~ 0 + treatment?







Hint





With ~ 0 + treatment there is no intercept column; instead you get one column per level, each acting as a per-group mean.









Solution






model.matrix(~ 0 + treatment, data = cond)

You get a matrix with two columns, treatmentDMSO and treatmentIC50, each with 1s for samples in that group and 0s otherwise (it is the second formulation from the lecture — \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\)). There is no overall intercept; each column directly estimates the log expression of that group. To get the IC50-vs-DMSO contrast you have to subtract the two coefficients explicitly:

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(round(cnt), cond, ~ 0 + treatment)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("treatment", "IC50", "DMSO"))
# or equivalently with a numeric contrast vector:
res <- results(dds, contrast = c(-1, 1))   # matches order of resultsNames

Same answer as the with-intercept version — just a different parametrisation.




QE2.8 A reviewer asks: “your design has 4 samples and 1 factor with 2 levels — how many parameters does your model actually estimate per gene?” Answer using the model matrix.







Hint





Number of parameters = number of columns of the model matrix. Residual degrees of freedom = \(n_\text{samples} - n_\text{params}\).









Solution





With ~ treatment and two levels, the model matrix has 2 columns (intercept + treatment indicator), so 2 parameters per gene. With 4 samples that leaves 2 residual degrees of freedom — exactly enough to estimate within-group variance from the 2 replicates per group. If you had only 1 replicate per group you would have 0 residual d.f. and DESeq2 would refuse to estimate dispersion.





Multivariate designs (extra)

QE3.1 Re-fit the E-MTAB-14822 dataset with an interaction term: design = ~ cell_type * treatment_duration. What extra coefficients show up in resultsNames(dds) compared to the additive ~ cell_type + treatment_duration model?







Hint





a * b is shorthand for a + b + a:b. The a:b term is the interaction.









Solution






dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(round(cnt), cond, ~ cell_type * treatment_duration)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
resultsNames(dds)

You get the same coefficients as the additive model plus one interaction coefficient per non-reference combination of the two factors (i.e. \((k_1-1)\times(k_2-1)\) extra columns in the model matrix, where \(k_i\) are the number of levels). Each interaction coefficient measures how much the treatment effect differs between cell lines — a non-zero value means the drug works differently in the two cell types.




QE3.2 Using resultsNames(dds) from the interaction model, pull out (a) the main effect of treatment in the reference cell line, and (b) the interaction term itself. What is the biological interpretation of each?







Hint





With an interaction, the treatment_duration_* coefficient is no longer the average treatment effect across cell lines — it is the treatment effect in the reference cell line only.









Solution






resultsNames(dds)
# (a) treatment effect in the reference cell line:
res_main <- results(dds, name = "treatment_duration_treated_vs_untreated")
# (b) interaction: how much bigger/smaller is the treatment effect in the other cell line
res_int  <- results(dds, name = "cell_typeX.treatment_durationtreated") # exact name from resultsNames


tells you which genes respond to the drug in the reference cell line. (b) tells you which genes respond differently in the second cell line vs. the reference — significant hits here are genes where the drug’s effect is cell-type-specific. Often what you actually want to report.





QE3.3 What is the practical difference between testing a main effect of treatment_duration and testing the interaction cell_type:treatment_duration? When would you prefer one over the other?







Hint





Think about the null hypothesis being tested in each case.









Solution






Main effect of treatment: \(H_0\) is “the drug has no effect” (in the reference cell line, when the model includes an interaction; or averaged across cell lines, in a purely additive model). Use this when you want a list of generally drug-responsive genes.
Interaction: \(H_0\) is “the drug effect is the same in both cell lines”. Significant interaction hits are genes whose response is cell-type-specific — e.g. potential resistance markers or selectivity markers.

You’d typically run both: main effect to find the drug’s general signature, interaction to find genes that explain differential sensitivity. A likelihood-ratio test (DESeq(dds, test = "LRT", reduced = ~ cell_type + treatment_duration)) lets you test the whole interaction block at once.
